3730:
A crone is an old woman — not just any old woman, but one who is seen as ugly, withered, and unpleasant. Think wrinkled skin, a bony frame, a sharp or bitter manner. That is the picture the word paints.

But "crone" is one of those words that wears different faces depending on where you encounter it, so knowing just the dictionary definition will leave you only partially equipped. Here is the full picture.
In everyday speech — it's an insult

In ordinary conversation, calling someone a crone is rude. It implies the woman is not merely old, but haggard — worn down, harsh, and sour. It is in the same family as words like "hag" or "old witch." If you say it about a real person, expect offense. This is the most common modern usage.
In folklore and fairy tales — it's an archetype

This is where the word truly lives. Across myths, folk tales, and fantasy stories from countless cultures, the crone is a familiar and recurring figure: the mysterious old woman who lives alone at the edge of the forest, the ancient fortune-teller who speaks in riddles, the witch who guards forbidden knowledge. She is always set apart from normal society — isolated, strange, and connected to something darker or deeper than ordinary life.

She can be a villain, like the old witch who lures children in Hansel and Gretel. She can be a helper, like the ancient woman who rewards a kind-hearted traveler with magical gifts. Sometimes she is both at once — terrifying and useful, frightening and wise. The most iconic crone in world folklore is probably Baba Yaga, the fearsome old woman of Slavic mythology who lives in a hut that stands on chicken legs and who can be either a destroyer or a guide, depending on how you approach her. The three witches in Shakespeare's Macbeth carry the same energy.

What defines the crone in storytelling is not just her age, but her position: she stands at the margins, between the world of the living and something beyond it. That liminal position gives her power.
In mythology and modern spirituality — it's a title of honor

In Wicca and neopagan spiritual traditions, the Crone is one of the three aspects of the feminine, alongside the Maiden and the Mother. The Maiden represents youth, new beginnings, and possibility. The Mother represents fertility, nurturing, and the fullness of life. The Crone represents old age, wisdom, endings, and transformation. She is associated with the waning moon, with winter, with death — and crucially, with a kind of deep, hard-won knowledge that only comes from having lived a full life.

In this framework, the Crone is not ugly or something to be feared. She is revered. Goddesses like Hecate, the Greek deity of witchcraft and crossroads, and the Morrígan, the Irish goddess of fate and death, are often understood as crone figures — ancient, powerful, standing at the threshold between life and death.
The modern reclaiming of the word

Some older women — particularly in feminist circles — have deliberately taken the word back and turned it into a source of pride. The logic goes like this: society calls older women crones as an insult because it sees their age as a loss — of beauty, of fertility, of social value. But these women argue that a crone is someone who has moved beyond needing society's approval, who has outlived expectations, and whose age is a form of power, not diminishment. Calling yourself a crone in this sense is an act of defiance and self-respect.
The full picture in one place

Depending on where you encounter "crone," it means one of three things. In everyday speech, it is a derogatory word for a disagreeable old woman — an insult, plain and simple. In stories and folklore, it is a powerful and ancient archetype: the old woman at the edge of the world who holds secrets, magic, and dangerous wisdom. In spiritual and feminist contexts, it is a title that honors the final and wisest stage of a woman's life.

Across all three uses, the word always points to extreme old age — concentrated, undisguised, stripped of pretense. What changes is whether that old age is seen as something ugly to be mocked, something mysterious to be respected, or something powerful to be claimed.
3731:
A crony is a close friend or associate of someone — but not just any friend. The word carries a strong negative meaning. A crony is specifically a friend who benefits from their connection to a powerful person in a way that is unfair, corrupt, or based on personal loyalty rather than merit.

The key idea is this: the crony doesn't earn their position, rewards, or opportunities through skill, hard work, or qualification. They get those things simply because they are friends with someone who has power — and that powerful person uses their position to help their friends at the expense of fairness.
What makes someone a "crony" and not just a "friend"?

This is the most important distinction.

If your friend helps you move to a new apartment, that's just a friend. But if a politician gives a massive government contract worth millions of rupees to his childhood friend's company — even though that company wasn't the best or most qualified — that childhood friend is now a crony.

Three things must be present for someone to be called a crony:

  1. A connection to someone powerful — a politician, a business executive, a ruler, a boss. Cronies almost always cluster around people who have power, money, or influence.
  2. Unfair benefit from that connection — the crony receives jobs, contracts, protection, promotions, favors, or other advantages that they did not earn on their own merits.
  3. The relationship is self-serving on both sides — the powerful person keeps their cronies close because it benefits them too. Cronies are loyal, they protect the powerful person's interests, and they don't ask too many difficult questions.
The emotional weight of the word

"Crony" is never a neutral or complimentary word. When you call someone a crony, you are implying:

  • They don't deserve what they have gotten.
  • They got ahead through connections and corruption, not talent or hard work.
  • There is something shady, unfair, or dishonest about the relationship.

If someone calls your friend your "crony," they are essentially saying: "This person is in your inner circle because it's convenient and mutually beneficial — not because they earned it."
Where is this word most commonly used?

Politics is the most natural home for this word. When a newly elected leader fills important government positions with personal friends, family members, or loyal supporters — regardless of whether those people are qualified — those people are called his cronies.

Business is the second major arena. When a CEO awards lucrative deals to companies run by his golf buddies, or when a board of directors protects an incompetent executive because he belongs to their social circle, those people are cronies.

You will almost never use "crony" to describe friendships in everyday life. It belongs to the world of power, money, and institutions.

• "The minister was accused of giving construction contracts worth billions to his old college cronies."
  • "After the new chairman took over, he quietly replaced the experienced team with his own cronies."
  • "The investigation revealed that the company had been run for years as a club for the CEO and his cronies."
  • "Voters were frustrated that the president seemed more interested in rewarding his cronies than solving the country's problems."

Once you understand "crony," the word cronyism follows naturally.

Cronyism is the system or practice of favoring one's cronies. It refers to the culture or habit — usually within an organization, government, or institution — of giving jobs, contracts, and power to friends and associates based on personal relationships rather than merit.

Think of it this way:

  • A crony is the person (the friend who benefits unfairly).
  • Cronyism is the behavior or system that produces such people.

"The company's rapid decline was blamed on years of cronyism at the top."

Imagine a ruler sitting at the center of a circle. The people inside that circle — the ones who get the contracts, the positions, the protection, the favors — are the cronies. They didn't get into that circle by being the most capable or deserving. They got in because the ruler trusts them personally, they've known each other for years, and each one helps protect the other's position. Anyone outside the circle — no matter how qualified — is simply left out.

That inner circle, in a word, is made up of cronies.

What it isA close associate of a powerful person who receives unfair benefits because of personal loyalty, not merit
ToneAlways negative — implies corruption, favoritism, unfairness
ContextPolitics, business, institutions — anywhere power is involved
Related wordCronyism — the practice of favoring one's cronies

The single sentence that captures it all: A crony is a friend of the powerful who profits from that friendship in ways they didn't earn — and the word is always used to criticize that arrangement.
3732:
Cronyism is when someone in a position of power gives jobs, contracts, favors, or opportunities to their close friends — not because those friends are the best or most qualified people for the job, but simply because they are friends.

The word comes from "crony," which is an informal word for a close, long-time friend or companion. So cronyism is essentially the practice of letting personal friendships drive important decisions that should be driven by skill, qualification, and fairness.

In a single sentence: cronyism is the abuse of power to reward your friends.

Imagine you are the mayor of a city, and your city needs to hire a construction company to build a new bridge. There are ten companies that apply. The right thing to do is to carefully review all ten companies, look at their experience, their prices, and the quality of their past work, and then choose the best one.

But instead, you choose your old college friend's company — even though their price is higher than others, their work history is weaker, and frankly, another company would have done a better job. You chose your friend simply because he is your friend, and because you want to do something good for him.

That is cronyism.

The key ingredients are always the same:

Power — The person practicing cronyism must be in a position of authority. They must have the ability to make decisions that affect others: hiring someone, awarding a contract, granting a license, handing out funds, or giving access to resources.

Personal relationships — The favor is given based on friendship, long-standing personal loyalty, or social closeness. These are people the decision-maker knows personally and feels warmly toward.

Bypassing merit — The decision ignores what is fair, what the rules say, or who is actually the most capable and deserving. The friendship outweighs everything else.

All three must be present. If a friend genuinely happens to be the most qualified candidate and gets the job after a fair process, that is not cronyism — that is just coincidence. Cronyism requires that the friendship is the reason for the decision, not just a coincidence alongside it.

Cronyism is most commonly talked about in two areas:

Politics and government: A newly elected politician appoints their old friends to important government positions — as advisors, ministers, ambassadors, or heads of agencies — regardless of whether those friends have the expertise to do the job well. Public money is used to fund projects that benefit companies owned by the politician's close associates. Government contracts are awarded to friendly businesses without open, competitive bidding.

Business and corporations: A CEO promotes their personal friends within the company over more talented employees. A board of directors hires an underqualified acquaintance into a senior role. A manager assigns the best projects, biggest bonuses, or plum assignments to people they socialise with, not to those who deserve it most.

Cronyism can also appear in smaller settings — universities, nonprofits, sports organizations, local clubs — anywhere that someone has power over decisions that affect others.
How Cronyism Differs from Similar Words

People often confuse cronyism with two related words: nepotism and favoritism. They are all members of the same family of ideas, but they are not identical.

Nepotism is specifically about favoring family members — hiring your cousin, promoting your sibling, or giving a contract to your spouse's company. The relationship is blood or marriage.

Favoritism is the broadest of the three. It simply means preferring certain people over others unfairly, for any personal reason — maybe you like someone's personality, maybe they remind you of yourself, maybe they always compliment you. It doesn't have to involve friendship or family specifically.

Cronyism sits in the middle. It is specifically about close friends and long-time associates — your inner circle, your old buddies, your trusted companions. It is favoritism, but of a particular kind: rooted in personal friendship and loyalty rather than family ties or vague personal preference.

Think of it this way: all cronyism is favoritism, but not all favoritism is cronyism. And nepotism involves family, while cronyism involves friends.

Cronyism is not just unfair to the individuals who deserved the opportunity but didn't get it. It causes damage at a much larger scale.

It puts incompetent people in important places. When skill stops mattering and friendship starts deciding who gets power, the result is that unqualified people end up running important things. A city's infrastructure is designed by an underqualified firm. A hospital is managed by someone with no medical administration experience. A government agency is led by someone who got the job because they went to school with the right person. The quality of outcomes drops.

It wastes resources. Public money, company funds, or organizational resources get directed toward people and projects chosen for personal reasons rather than value and effectiveness. Money that could have built a better bridge, funded more research, or created more jobs gets funneled to friends instead.

It kills morale and destroys trust. When workers see that hard work and talent don't determine who gets ahead — but rather who the boss drinks coffee with — they lose motivation. People who genuinely try to do a good job feel cheated and undervalued. The best people often leave, because they realize merit doesn't matter here.

It corrupts systems. Cronyism, over time, builds a culture where loyalty to a person matters more than loyalty to rules, standards, or the public good. It erodes the institutions that are supposed to protect fairness — hiring processes, bidding systems, regulatory oversight. Once cronyism becomes normalized, it is very hard to root out.

It breeds more cronyism. The friends who are rewarded often return the favor. They hire their friends. They give contracts back to the person who helped them. A web of mutual back-scratching develops, and the system increasingly serves insiders at the expense of everyone else.

Cronyism is not always obvious, because it often disguises itself as normal decision-making. But there are signs to watch for:

When hiring or promotion decisions consistently seem to favor people with personal connections to the decision-maker, rather than people with stronger track records or qualifications, cronyism may be at work.

When contracts or deals are awarded without open competition — or when the same companies keep winning bids despite not being obviously the best choice — it is worth asking whether personal relationships are involved.

When a new leader comes in and quickly surrounds themselves with old friends rather than experienced professionals, and when those friends receive salaries, titles, or authority that seems disproportionate to their credentials, cronyism is likely happening.

When criticism of the leader or the organization is handled by protecting friends and punishing outsiders — rather than being dealt with based on the facts — it is often a sign that cronyism has taken deep root.

Cronyism represents a collision between two different ideas of how the world should work.

One idea is meritocracy — the belief that people should rise or succeed based on their talent, effort, and results. The best person gets the job. The strongest proposal wins the contract. Outcomes are earned.

The other idea — the one cronyism runs on — is loyalty and personal connection. Who you know. Who trusts you. Who owes you a favor. Who you've been friends with for thirty years.

In an ideal world, personal friendships are wonderful things — but they stay in their lane. They don't intrude into professional decisions that affect the public, other workers, or the integrity of institutions. Cronyism happens when that boundary breaks down, and personal loyalty starts overriding fairness, rules, and the greater good.

This is why cronyism is universally seen as a negative and unethical practice. It is not just unfair to individuals — it hollows out the systems and institutions that societies depend on.
3733: "Crooked" has two distinct meanings — one physical, one moral — and both are important and widely used. Let's cover each one completely.
Meaning 1: Not straight; bent, twisted, or uneven

"Crooked" describes anything that deviates from being straight, flat, level, or properly aligned. If something should be straight but isn't — if it bends, curves, leans, or sits at the wrong angle — it is crooked.

Think of a nail hammered badly into wood. Instead of going straight in, it bends to one side. That nail is crooked. Think of an old mountain road that constantly curves left and right instead of going straight. That road is crooked. Think of a picture frame hanging on a wall but tilted slightly to one side. That picture is hanging crooked.

The word covers a wide range of "not-straightness" — a single bend, a twist, a curve, a lean, an angle that's off. It doesn't matter whether something is a little off or a lot off; both can be called crooked.

More examples:

  • Crooked teeth — teeth that grow in irregular directions instead of straight
  • A crooked nose — a nose that is bent, often from being broken at some point
  • A crooked spine — a spine that curves sideways instead of running straight down the back
  • Crooked handwriting — letters that go up and down unevenly rather than following a straight line
  • A crooked path through the forest — a path that winds and turns constantly

One nuance worth knowing: We tend to use "crooked" when something looks off or should be straight but isn't. A river naturally curves and winds, and in everyday speech people freely call it "a crooked river." But if an engineer designs a road with planned curves, you'd typically call those "curves" or "bends," not crookedness — though informally, "crooked road" is still very common and widely understood.

The second meaning is figurative — based on a very old and natural human idea: a straight path = honesty and goodness; going off the straight path = dishonesty and moral failure. So just as something physically "crooked" bends away from the straight line, a person who is morally "crooked" bends away from honesty and the law.

In this sense, "crooked" means fraudulent, corrupt, or criminal — acting dishonestly for personal gain, often by abusing a position of trust or power. It's a strong, accusatory word.

Examples:

  • A crooked politician takes bribes, abuses power, or manipulates the system for personal benefit instead of serving the public.
  • A crooked cop is a police officer who breaks the very laws they're supposed to enforce — perhaps accepting bribes to look the other way, or falsifying evidence.
  • A crooked deal is a business transaction built on deception, where one party is being cheated.
  • A crooked accountant falsifies financial records — perhaps to help a client evade taxes or hide stolen money.
  • A crooked scheme is a fraudulent plan designed to trick people out of money or rights.

This meaning is informal in register — very natural in everyday speech, in journalism, and in novels, but in formal legal documents or academic papers, you'd more often see words like corrupt, fraudulent, or dishonest. That said, "crooked" is completely standard, widely understood, and carries real punch when used.
How do you always know which meaning is being used?

Context makes it almost impossible to confuse the two:

  • If the sentence is about a physical object — a road, a nail, a tooth, a frame, a tree — it's the physical meaning.
  • If the sentence is about a person, an organization, a deal, or a plan — it's almost certainly the dishonesty meaning.

"The old fence was completely crooked" → physically bent and uneven.
"That real estate agent is completely crooked" → dishonest and likely criminal.

You will almost never encounter a sentence where both meanings seem equally possible. Context resolves it immediately, every time.

This phrase deserves its own mention because it's extremely common and it can surprise learners. A crooked smile (or crooked grin) is purely physical — it means one side of the mouth is raised higher than the other, making the smile lopsided or asymmetrical. It has nothing to do with dishonesty. In fact, in literature and everyday speech, a crooked smile is very often described as charming, roguish, or attractive. You'll encounter it constantly in novels and films, so it's worth remembering.

The word crook, as a noun, directly shares the dishonest meaning of "crooked." A crook is simply a dishonest person or a criminal. "Don't trust him — he's a crook." If someone calls a person crooked, they're calling them a crook.

• Crookedly (adverb): The painting hung crookedly. / He smiled crookedly at her.
  • Crookedness (noun): The crookedness of the hallway made it hard to move furniture. / The crookedness of local government officials made headlines.

Like most adjectives, "crooked" works with degree modifiers:

  • Slightly crooked — barely off-straight, or mildly dishonest
  • Very crooked / deeply crooked — severely bent, or profoundly corrupt
  • Completely crooked / thoroughly crooked — entirely dishonest, corrupt through and through
The single most important thing to remember

If you remember only one thing: "crooked" means "off the straight line" — physically bent in the case of objects, and morally bent in the case of people and their actions. That one core idea ties both meanings together beautifully and makes the word easy to feel intuitively, not just memorize.
3734: To croon means to sing in a soft, low, smooth, and gentle voice. The singing is quiet rather than loud, warm rather than sharp, and flows effortlessly — like honey poured slowly. The overall feeling is tender, intimate, and soothing. It's the voice of someone drawing a listener close, not performing for a stadium.

The word sing is broad and neutral — it simply means to make musical sounds with your voice. Croon is far more specific. It tells you how someone is singing: softly, smoothly, gently, and with emotional warmth.

If someone is belting a song at the top of their lungs, that is the opposite of crooning. If someone is screeching, or even just singing in a plain, flat, emotionless way, that is not crooning either. Crooning requires a specific combination of gentleness, smoothness, and warmth — all at once.

Crooning is almost always tied to gentle, tender emotion — romantic, sentimental, or soothing. Think of:

  • A mother softly singing a lullaby to a sleeping baby
  • A classic singer performing a love song in a dimly lit, intimate room
  • Someone humming tenderly and quietly to themselves or to a person they love

The emotion behind crooning is never harsh, frantic, or energetic. It is always calm, affectionate, and close.
The Two Main Contexts You'll See It

In music: Crooning is strongly associated with a style of singing made famous by classic performers — those known for their warm, buttery, smooth voices delivering romantic songs with quiet intimacy. This is where the noun "crooner" comes from — a singer who specialises in this style. Legendary names like Frank Sinatra, Bing Crosby, and Dean Martin are considered the definitive crooners. Calling someone a crooner is almost always a compliment: it means their voice is velvety, effortless, and emotionally rich.

In everyday life: You don't have to be a professional singer to croon. A parent can croon to their child. Someone can croon softly to themselves while doing the dishes. The word just means that the singing (or humming) is being done in that gentle, low, unhurried way.

Yes, loosely. "Croon" can occasionally describe speaking — but only when the speaking has that same soft, cooing, affectionate quality. For example: "He crooned sweet nothings into her ear." Here it means he spoke softly and tenderly, almost musically. But this is a figurative use — the core meaning always lives in singing.

• "She crooned a lullaby until the baby drifted off to sleep."
  • "The old jazz singer crooned beautifully into the microphone."
  • "He crooned love songs in a warm, velvety voice that filled the room."
  • "She crooned softly to herself as she walked home."

Very rarely, croon can carry a mild suggestion that someone's singing is overly sentimental or a little too smooth — almost artificially sweet. But this is uncommon and context-dependent. In the overwhelming majority of cases, it is either neutral or warmly complimentary.
One Simple Image to Lock It In

Imagine a dial that goes from "whispering" on one end to "screaming" on the other. Crooning sits close to the soft, quiet end — but it's not just quiet. It has musical warmth, smoothness, and tenderness baked into it. If a voice feels like a gentle hug, it's probably a croon.
3735: Croquet is an outdoor lawn game in which players use long-handled wooden hammers (called mallets) to hit coloured balls across a grass field, trying to pass them through a series of small wire hoops stuck into the ground. Those hoops are called wickets (or hoops). The goal is to be the first to drive your ball through all the wickets on the course, in the correct order, and finish at a designated peg or post.

Picture a well-kept, flat grassy lawn — the kind you'd see in a classic English garden. Several metal wire hoops (wickets) are pushed into the ground at various spots across the lawn, forming a course. Players stand with a mallet — which looks a bit like a golf club, but with a flat cylindrical head — and strike their ball along the ground. There is no throwing or catching involved. Everything is done by hitting.

Each player has their own ball, usually in a distinct colour — red, blue, black, or yellow — so you can always tell whose ball is whose.

On your turn, you hit your ball and try to guide it through the next wicket in the sequence. If your ball passes cleanly through a wicket, you earn an extra hit. This is important because skilled players can chain several hits together in a single turn, moving their ball a great distance around the course while their opponents get no chance to play.

Here's where strategy comes in: if your ball strikes another player's ball, you get a roquet, which gives you two bonus hits. You can use one of those hits to knock the opponent's ball far away from their ideal position — sending it into a tricky corner, near an edge, or just far from the next wicket. This is one of the most tactical and satisfying parts of croquet. You're not just trying to advance your own ball; you're also trying to disrupt others.

Croquet is a game of precision, patience, and cunning. It looks gentle and slow-paced on the surface — people walking calmly across a lawn, tapping balls — but beneath that calm exterior, it involves careful planning and sharp decision-making. Every hit counts. Do you advance your own ball, or do you use your turn to exile an opponent's ball to a bad spot? These small decisions build up into the outcome of the whole game.

This contrast between its polite, leisurely appearance and its surprisingly tactical depth is one of the things croquet is most famous for. It has a reputation as a refined, even aristocratic pastime, historically associated with country houses and garden parties in Britain.

There are a few main versions of the game played around the world:

Association Croquet — the classic, formal version played internationally. The full course has six wickets and two pegs. This is the version used in competitive and club play, and it has the deepest tactical complexity.

Golf Croquet — a simpler, faster version where each player competes to be the first to get their ball through each hoop. There is no rushing opponents' balls away; each hoop is a mini-contest in itself. This version is more accessible for casual players and beginners.

Garden or Backyard Croquet — the informal version most people encounter at parties or picnics. Rules are relaxed, the course may be irregular, and the emphasis is on fun rather than strict competition.

A full croquet set typically includes:

  • Mallets — one per player. The mallet's head is cylindrical, with flat faces on both ends for striking, and it sits at the end of a long handle. Players stand with the mallet between their legs and swing it like a pendulum.
  • Balls — solid, heavy, and coloured. Croquet balls are considerably heavier than they look, which helps them roll smoothly on grass.
  • Wickets (hoops) — U-shaped metal arches pushed into the ground. The ball must pass through the opening of the arch.
  • Pegs (stakes) — a central or finishing post that balls must hit to complete the course.

The word croquet is also widely known from Lewis Carroll's famous novel Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, in which the Queen of Hearts hosts an absurd croquet game using flamingos as mallets and hedgehogs as balls — a playful mockery of the game's prim, rule-bound nature.

In everyday English, when someone calls a game of croquet "cutthroat," they mean it seriously — players can and do ruthlessly knock opponents' balls to the far corners of the lawn, ruining carefully built positions in one stroke. This ruthless tactical edge is considered perfectly acceptable, even skillful, in the game.

Croquet (noun) is a precision lawn game where players use mallets to hit balls through hoops in a set order, with the freedom to strategically disrupt opponents along the way. It is simultaneously a leisurely garden pastime and a surprisingly deep tactical game, depending on the level at which it is played.
3736:
A cross is a shape made by two straight lines or bars that meet and intersect each other — one going up-and-down (vertical) and one going left-and-right (horizontal). Picture the plus sign (+), or the letter "t". That is the most basic, visual meaning of the word.

Everything else about this word flows from this shape, its history, or the idea of two things coming together.

1. The Shape Itself

A cross is any figure formed by two lines or bars that cross each other. The vertical part and the horizontal part meet somewhere in the middle — though not always at the exact center.

There are different varieties:

  • A Latin cross (the most common): the vertical bar is longer than the horizontal one, like a lowercase "t" stretched out. This is what you typically picture when someone says "a cross."
  • A Greek cross: all four arms are of equal length, like a + sign.
  • An X-shaped cross (called a "saltire"): the bars cross diagonally, like the letter X.

The cross shape appears everywhere in daily life — as a symbol, a marker, a design — and all of the meanings below are connected to this same fundamental form.

2. The Christian Cross

This is probably the most widely known meaning.

Roughly two thousand years ago, the Roman Empire executed a man named Jesus of Nazareth by nailing him to a large wooden cross and leaving him to die. This method of execution was called crucifixion, and it was one of the cruelest punishments of the ancient world.

Christians believe that Jesus died for the sins of all humanity, and that through his death and resurrection (coming back to life), people could be forgiven and saved. Because of this, the cross became the defining symbol of Christianity — representing sacrifice, redemption, love, and hope.

Today, you see crosses:

  • On top of churches and cathedrals
  • As jewelry (necklaces, rings, bracelets)
  • On gravestones and in cemeteries
  • In Christian art, paintings, and architecture
  • Tattooed on people as an expression of faith

In this meaning, the word "cross" carries enormous religious and emotional weight. It is not just a shape — it is a symbol of an entire belief system, a relationship with God, and the promise of eternal life.

3. The Actual Instrument of Execution

Before it became a holy symbol, the cross was a very real, physical object — a large wooden structure used by the Romans to execute people.

The condemned person was forced to carry the heavy wooden beam to the place of execution, where they were nailed through the wrists and feet to the cross, which was then stood upright. Death came slowly, through exhaustion and suffocation.

So when you read historical texts, the Bible, or any account of ancient Roman punishment, "the cross" refers to this actual, terrifying wooden structure.

4. A Burden or Trial (Figurative)

Because Jesus carried his own cross on the way to his execution, and because the cross represents suffering, the word has taken on a powerful figurative meaning:

A cross = a heavy burden, a hardship, or a source of suffering that a person must endure throughout their life.

It is usually something painful that cannot easily be escaped — a chronic illness, a difficult family member, a lifelong sacrifice, or an unavoidable responsibility.

Examples:

  • "His addiction has been a heavy cross to bear."
  • "Caring for her aging parents alone has been her cross in life."

The phrase "to bear one's cross" or "to carry one's cross" means to endure one's hardship with patience and without complaining — just as Jesus carried his cross without giving up.

5. A Hybrid — A Mix of Two Things

When two different animals, plants, or varieties are bred together, the result is called a cross.

  • A mule is a cross between a horse and a donkey.
  • A liger is a cross between a lion and a tiger.
  • Many modern apples, roses, and vegetables are crosses between two parent varieties, bred to bring out the best features of each.

The idea is that something new is created by combining two distinct things — just as two lines form a cross by meeting in the middle.

This meaning extends informally beyond biology:

  • "That restaurant serves a cross between Italian and Japanese food."
  • "Her management style is a cross between strict discipline and warm encouragement."

In this usage, "a cross between A and B" simply means something that blends or combines A and B.

6. A Medal or Award Shaped Like a Cross

Many of the world's most prestigious military honors, decorations, and awards are physically shaped like a cross. When someone refers to these, "cross" is part of the name.

Examples:

  • The Victoria Cross — the highest military honor in the United Kingdom, awarded for extraordinary bravery in battle.
  • The Iron Cross — a famous German military decoration, used across different historical periods.
  • The George Cross — a British civilian bravery award.

In this sense, "a cross" is a medal — a physical award pinned to a uniform or kept as a symbol of honor.

7. A Monument, Marker, or Memorial

A cross can also refer to a physical object — usually made of stone, wood, or metal — that is erected in a public or sacred space as a monument, memorial, or landmark.

You encounter these as:

  • Grave markers: Simple crosses in cemeteries marking where someone is buried.
  • Roadside crosses: Small crosses placed at the site of a road accident to memorialize someone who died there.
  • Market crosses: Historical stone cross structures in the central squares of old British and European towns, where markets were traditionally held. Many still stand today as heritage monuments.
  • Wayside crosses: Crosses placed along roads and pathways in religious communities, especially in Catholic regions of Europe, as points of prayer and blessing for travelers.

8. In Sport: Boxing

In boxing, a cross is one of the four fundamental punches. Specifically, it is a powerful, straight punch thrown across the front of the body with your rear (dominant) hand.

If you are right-handed, your right hand is in the back position, and a right cross is a straight, strong punch aimed directly at the opponent, crossing the center line of your body. It is one of the hardest-hitting punches because the power of your entire body rotation is behind it.

You will often hear phrases like "a right cross", "he landed a sharp cross", or "a jab-cross combination."

9. In Sport: Football (Soccer)

In football (soccer), a cross is a pass played from a wide position — near the sideline or the "wing" of the field — into the central area in front of the opponent's goal (called the penalty box or the box).

The purpose is to deliver the ball into a dangerous area where attacking teammates can attempt to score, usually by heading the ball or striking it on the volley.

You will hear phrases like "he sent in a brilliant cross", "the cross found the striker at the far post", or "she whipped in a low cross."

10. On Flags, Emblems, and Symbols

The cross shape is deeply embedded in the visual identity of many nations, organizations, and institutions.

  • The Union Jack (the national flag of the United Kingdom) is composed of three overlapping crosses: the red cross of St. George (England), the white diagonal cross of St. Andrew (Scotland), and the red diagonal cross of St. Patrick (Ireland).
  • The Swiss flag features a bold white cross on a red background.
  • The Red Cross (officially the International Committee of the Red Cross) is one of the world's largest humanitarian organizations, and its emblem is a red cross on a white background — a symbol of neutral, impartial medical and humanitarian aid in conflict zones.
  • The flag of Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Iceland all feature a cross (known as the "Nordic cross").

In heraldry (the art of designing coats of arms), crosses appear in hundreds of different variations and carry their own symbolic meanings depending on the form and color.

It helps to see how all these meanings are related:

The shape (two lines crossing) is the root of everything.

That shape was used to build the instrument of execution on which Jesus died.

That death gave the shape its religious and spiritual meaning for Christians.

From the suffering of carrying the cross came the figurative meaning of a personal burden.

The respected and sacred nature of the cross inspired medals and honors to take that shape.

The same shape inspired monuments, memorials, and national symbols.

The idea of two things coming together and creating something new gave us the biological and informal meaning of a hybrid or mixture.

And the visual image of something moving across from one side toward a central point gave us the sports meanings in boxing and football.

ContextWhat "cross" means
General / VisualA shape formed by two intersecting lines
ChristianityThe symbol of the Christian faith; what Jesus died on
HistoryThe actual Roman wooden execution device
FigurativeA personal burden or lifelong hardship
Biology / InformalA hybrid; something combining two different things
AwardsA medal or honor shaped like a cross
MonumentsA physical cross structure used as a grave marker or memorial
BoxingA straight punch thrown with the rear (dominant) hand
Football/SoccerA pass from the wing into the center of the field
Flags & SymbolsA cross-shaped emblem on a flag, coat of arms, or institutional logo

That is the complete picture of cross as a noun — from its most concrete, physical meaning to its most abstract, spiritual, and sporting ones. Every time you encounter the word, you can now ask: is this about the shape, the religion, the burden, the hybrid, or the sport? — and you will have the tools to understand it fully.

A crossbreed is a living thing — an animal or a plant — that is born from two parents who belong to different breeds or varieties of the same species.

Think of it this way: if a purebred Labrador dog mates with a purebred Poodle, the puppies born from them are crossbreeds. They are not fully Labradors, and they are not fully Poodles. They are something in between — a new kind of animal that carries traits from both parents.

To really understand "crossbreed," you first need to understand what a breed is.

Within a single species — say, dogs — there are many different varieties that humans have developed over generations. A German Shepherd, a Beagle, a Bulldog — these are all dogs (same species), but they look different, behave differently, and have different physical traits. Each of these distinct varieties is called a breed.

Now, when two animals from different breeds mate and produce an offspring, that offspring is a crossbreed. The crossbreed inherits a mix of characteristics from both its parents.
The Key Point: What Makes It a "Crossbreed"

The word "crossbreed" (noun) specifically refers to the resulting offspring — the actual animal or plant that was born. It is not the process of mating; it is the product of that mating.

So if someone says, "That dog is a crossbreed," they mean: that dog was born to parents of two different breeds.

Dogs are the most common example people think of:

  • A Labradoodle is a crossbreed — its parents are a Labrador Retriever and a Poodle.
  • A Cockapoo is a crossbreed — its parents are a Cocker Spaniel and a Poodle.
  • A Goldendoodle is a crossbreed — its parents are a Golden Retriever and a Poodle.
  • A Puggle is a crossbreed — its parents are a Pug and a Beagle.

Plants can be crossbreeds too:

  • Many modern varieties of roses, apples, or wheat are crossbreeds, created by combining two different varieties to get a plant with better qualities — more colour, sweeter fruit, or greater resistance to disease.

These two words are direct opposites, and understanding one makes the other clearer.

  • A purebred animal has parents that are both of the same breed. A puppy born to two German Shepherds is a purebred German Shepherd.
  • A crossbreed animal has parents that are of two different breeds. A puppy born to a German Shepherd and a Husky is a crossbreed.

Purebreds are considered "pure" in the sense that their ancestry stays within one specific breed for many generations. Crossbreeds, on the other hand, bring together two different breed lines.

You will often hear the word hybrid used similarly. The two words overlap in meaning and are frequently used interchangeably in everyday speech. However, there is a subtle traditional distinction:

  • Crossbreed usually refers to offspring of two different breeds or varieties within the same species (e.g., two types of dogs, two varieties of wheat).
  • Hybrid can sometimes refer to offspring of two entirely different species (e.g., a mule, which comes from a horse and a donkey — two distinct species).

In casual conversation, though, most people use both words to mean roughly the same thing: an offspring from two genetically different parents.

Crossbreeds are often created deliberately by humans for specific reasons:

  • To combine the best traits of two breeds (e.g., the intelligence of a Poodle + the friendliness of a Labrador)
  • To produce animals or plants that are healthier or stronger (this is sometimes called hybrid vigour — the idea that mixing breeds can result in offspring that are more resilient than either parent)
  • To create animals suited for specific tasks or environments
  • To develop new crop varieties with higher yield or better nutrition

• "The shelter was full of crossbreeds that needed homes."
  • "Her dog was a crossbreed — part Border Collie, part Springer Spaniel."
  • "Many of the crops grown today are carefully developed crossbreeds."
  • "He wasn't sure of the dog's exact parentage, but it was clearly some kind of crossbreed."
A crossbreed is an animal or plant that comes from two parents of different breeds or varieties, and it typically carries a mix of traits from both.

A crosshair is a fine, thin line — or more commonly, a pair of two such lines crossing each other at their centers to form a "+" shape — used as a reference point for aiming, targeting, or aligning something precisely.

Think of it as a visual anchor. It tells your eye: "This exact center point is where your focus should be."

Picture the plus sign: +

Two straight lines — one running left to right (horizontal), one running top to bottom (vertical) — meet and cross at a single point in the middle. That meeting point, the dead center, is the most important part. It is what you align with whatever you are aiming at or measuring.

Sometimes the lines are solid all the way through. Sometimes there is a small gap or a dot at the center to make it even easier to pinpoint the exact spot.

Crosshairs appear in two broad worlds: the physical (real-life optical tools) and the digital (screens and software).

In physical/optical devices:

  • Rifle scopes and gun sights — A soldier or hunter looks through the scope and sees crosshairs. They align the center of the crosshairs with their target before firing. The crosshair tells them exactly where the bullet will land.
  • Telescopes — Astronomers use crosshairs inside telescope eyepieces to pinpoint the exact location of a star or planet.
  • Microscopes — Scientists use them to measure or mark a precise location on a specimen under the lens.
  • Surveying instruments — Engineers and land surveyors use crosshairs in their devices (like a theodolite) to take exact measurements of land and distances.
  • Camera viewfinders — Some cameras display crosshairs to help the photographer frame and focus a shot precisely.

In digital and virtual environments:

  • Video games — Almost every shooting game shows a crosshair on screen, overlaid on whatever the player's character is pointing their weapon at. It is your aiming guide in the virtual world.
  • Computer cursors — In image-editing software like Photoshop, or in technical drawing programs, the regular arrow cursor sometimes changes into a crosshair shape. This happens when pixel-perfect precision is needed — for example, when you are selecting an exact point on an image.
  • Graphical user interfaces (GUIs) — In software that deals with maps, charts, or precision design, a crosshair cursor helps the user click or interact with a very specific location.
What Is the Purpose of a Crosshair?

The purpose is always the same: precision.

Whenever a task requires you to identify, aim at, or align with an exact point — not roughly, not approximately, but exactly — a crosshair gives your eye a clear, unambiguous reference. Without it, you are guessing. With it, you have a precise guide.

Both the singular (crosshair) and plural (crosshairs) forms exist, and you will encounter both.

  • Crosshair (singular) technically refers to one of the individual lines.
  • Crosshairs (plural) refers to the full crossing pattern — both lines together as a single system.

In everyday usage, "crosshairs" (plural) is far more common, even when referring to the symbol as a whole. People rarely say "I put the crosshair on the target." They almost always say "I put the crosshairs on the target." The plural form has become the standard, natural way to refer to the entire thing.

Beyond its literal, physical meaning, "crosshairs" has a widely used figurative meaning in everyday language. This is possibly as common as its literal meaning, so you must know it.

To be in someone's crosshairs (or in the crosshairs) means to be the target of someone's focused attention, criticism, scrutiny, or hostility. It suggests that someone has "aimed" their full focus at you — usually with an intent that is threatening, aggressive, or at least intensely serious.

It comes directly from the idea of a shooter placing a target in the center of their rifle's crosshairs before pulling the trigger. To be in the crosshairs is to be in that dangerous, targeted position.

Examples of figurative use:

  • "After the financial scandal, the CEO found himself squarely in the crosshairs of government regulators."
    → Regulators were now intensely focused on him, investigating and targeting him.
  • "Small businesses have been in the crosshairs of rising inflation for months."
    → Inflation has been severely affecting and "targeting" small businesses.
  • "The rival company is in our crosshairs — we plan to compete directly with them this year."
    → The company has made the rival their specific, focused target.

The figurative use can imply anything from criticism and investigation to competition and rivalry to outright danger and threat, depending on the context. The core idea is always the same: someone or something has become a deliberate, focused target.

• "The sniper peered through his scope and placed the crosshairs on the distant target."
  • "In the video game, a red crosshair appeared on screen whenever the player aimed at an enemy."
  • "The cursor changed to a crosshair when she zoomed into the image to select a single pixel."
  • "The astronomer carefully adjusted the telescope until the star sat perfectly at the center of the crosshairs."

A crosshair is a "+" shaped marking used to pinpoint an exact location for aiming or precision, seen in scopes, games, and software — and in everyday language, to be "in the crosshairs" means to be someone's focused target.
3739:
A crossing guard is a person whose job is to help people — especially children — cross a road safely. They stand at a specific spot on the road, stop the traffic when needed, and signal to people when it is safe to walk across.

Think of them as a human traffic controller, but their only focus is making sure people on foot get across the road without getting hurt.

A crossing guard does not just stand and watch. They actively control traffic and people:

  • They step into the road and hold up a handheld stop sign (a paddle-shaped sign that says "STOP") or raise their hand firmly to signal drivers to stop.
  • Once the vehicles have stopped, they signal to the pedestrians — usually with a wave or a nod — that it is now safe to cross.
  • They sometimes walk across with the people, especially with young children, to make sure everyone reaches the other side.
  • They keep a close watch for drivers who are not slowing down or who might ignore the signal.
  • After everyone has crossed, they step back onto the pavement and allow traffic to move again.

In many countries, crossing guards have legal authority to stop traffic. This means drivers are legally required to obey their stop signal, just as they would obey a traffic light or a police officer directing traffic.

Crossing guards are stationed at pedestrian crossings — the marked areas on the road where people are supposed to walk across (also called crosswalks or zebra crossings). You will most commonly find them:

  • Near schools — this is by far the most common location, because children walk to and from school and need extra protection near roads.
  • At busy intersections where traffic is heavy and crossing is risky, even for adults.
  • In areas with poor visibility, such as roads with bends or obstructions, where drivers may not see pedestrians in time.

Crossing guards do not work all day. Their hours are tied to when pedestrian traffic is highest near their assigned spot:

  • Morning, when children and commuters are heading to school or work.
  • Afternoon, when school ends and children walk back home.
  • Sometimes during lunch break, if students are allowed to leave the school grounds midday.

This means a crossing guard's working day is often split into two or three short blocks of time, not a continuous shift.

Crossing guards are easy to spot:

  • They wear brightly coloured vests — usually orange, yellow, or lime green — with reflective strips that catch the light. This makes them visible to drivers from a distance, even in poor weather or low light.
  • They carry a handheld stop sign, which is a paddle or round sign on a stick. In the United Kingdom, this sign is round and orange, and people often call crossing guards "lollipop men" or "lollipop women" because the sign resembles a giant lollipop.
  • Some crossing guards also wear a uniform, a cap, or a badge that identifies their official role.

Crossing guards can be:

  • Paid workers hired by a school district, a city government, or a local council.
  • Volunteers, such as parents of students or retired community members who take on this role out of goodwill.
  • In some schools, particularly in older traditions, senior students are assigned the role on a rotating basis — they are often called "school patrol" or "safety patrol" members.

Crossing guards are not police officers, but they carry out a small, specific piece of what traffic police do — managing the safe movement of people at a crossing point.

You might wonder: don't traffic lights handle this? Sometimes, yes. But:

  • Not every crossing has a traffic light, especially near schools in quieter neighbourhoods.
  • Children are not always good judges of traffic speed and distance. A crossing guard removes the need for a child to make that judgement call.
  • Drivers pay more attention to a person standing in the road than to painted lines on the ground.
  • Traffic patterns near schools are unpredictable — cars park, buses stop, children run. A human presence helps manage the chaos.

In short, crossing guards exist because some situations are too complex or too risky to be handled by road markings and traffic lights alone. A human being who can assess the situation in real time and react is safer.

• "The crossing guard held up her stop sign and the cars came to a halt so the children could cross."
  • "He worked as a crossing guard outside the primary school for over ten years."
  • "The crossing guard waved the children across and then stepped back onto the pavement."
  • "On rainy mornings, the crossing guard wore a bright yellow raincoat over her vest."
  • "The city hired two new crossing guards for the busy intersection near the high school."

A crossing guard is a safety worker stationed at a road crossing — most often near a school — whose job is to stop traffic and help people, especially children, cross the road safely. They wear bright, visible clothing, carry a handheld stop sign, work during peak pedestrian hours, and often have the legal authority to require drivers to stop. They exist because painted crosswalks and traffic lights alone are not always enough to protect people — especially young children — from the dangers of road traffic.
